DNA is the genetic material in all living organ- isms RNA is genetic material in some viruses Long Polymer Chain Shorter Polymer Chain Life of DNA is longer Its life is short DNA occurs only in one form in any organism 3 types of RNA are present in an organism: - mRNA, rRNA, tRNA DNA is functional in the transmission of genetic in- formation It forms as a media for long-term storage RNA is functional is the transmission of the genetic code that is necessary for the protein creation from the nucleus to the ribosome Bases present are Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, & Thymine Bases present are Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine & Uracil Genome x A genome is the DNA, or sequence of genes, in a cell. x Most of the DNA is in the nucleus and intricately coiled into a structure called the chromosome. x The rest is in the mitochondria, the cell’s powerhouse, and some is chloroplast DNA. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 126 x Every human cell contains a pair of chromosomes, each of which has three billion base pairs or one of four molecules – adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C) – that pair in precise ways. x The order of base pairs & varying lengths of these sequences constitute the “genes”, which are respon- sible for making amino acids, proteins and, thereby, everything that is necessary for the body to function. x When these genes are altered (mutated), proteins sometimes do not function as intended, leading to disease. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 127 Genome Sequencing x Sequencing a genome means deciphering the exact order of base pairs in an individual. x This “deciphering” or reading of the genome is what sequencing is all about. x In this particular piece of DNA, an adenine (A) is followed by a guanine (G), which is followed by a thymine (T), which in turn is followed by a cytosine (C), another cytosine (C), and so on. Whole genome sequencing x Exome, the portion of the genes responsible for making proteins occupies just about 1% of the actual gene. x Rather than sequence the whole gene, many geneticists rely on “exome maps”. x However, the non-exome portions also affect the functioning of the genes. x Hence to know which genes of a person’s DNA are “mutated” the whole genome sequencing is required. x Whole genome sequencing is the process of determining the complete DNA sequence of an organism's genome at a single time. x This entails sequencing all of an organism's chromosomal DNA as well as DNA contained in the mitochon- dria and, for plants, in the chloroplast. x In practice, genome sequences that are nearly complete are also called whole genome sequences. x The whole genome sequencing relies on new technologies that allow rapid sequencing of the entire genome in a matter of a few days. Benefits of Genome Sequencing x Whole genome sequencing data of a person can be analysed to determine if they carry genes for particular single genetic disorders (caused due to mutation). This will help usher in a new era of personalized medicine. Stem Cell or Cord Blood Banking Stem Cells x The blood collected from the umbilical cord of the new-born is a rich source of stem cells. x The stem cells are unspecialised cells (they do not have a specific predefined function). Stem cell banking or Cord blood (umbilical cord blood) Banking x Cord blood is the blood that remains in the umbilical cord and placenta post-delivery. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 128 x Cord blood at the time of delivery a rich source of stem cells and other cells of the immune system. x Cord blood banking is the process of collecting the cord blood and extracting and cryogenically freezing its stem cells and other cells of the immune system for potential future medical use. x In some parts of the world, cord blood banking is more often referred to as stem cell banking. x Cord blood banking is designed to collect the stem cells and not the actual blood cells themselves. How long can the stem cells be preserved? x The stem cells are preserved in liquid nitrogen in cord blood banks. x Technically, there is no expiry date and these stem cells can be preserved for a lifetime. x Scientifically, evidence exists that they can be stored for about 20 years. Why are stem cells special? x In some organs, such as the bone marrow, stem cells regularly divide to repair and replace damaged tissues. x Stem cells taken from umbilical cord blood are like those taken from bone marrow, capable of pro- ducing all blood cells: red cells, platelets, and immune system cells. x That is, they are capable of renewing themselves through cell division to give rise to new stem cells or specialized cell types (bone cells, muscle cells, etc.). What are the uses of stem cells? x In a patient, they can be induced to become tissue- or organ-specific cells with special functions. x Hence, they offer the possibility of a renewable source of replacement cells and tissues to treat diseases including macular degeneration, spinal cord injury, stroke, burns, heart disease, diabetes, etc. x The stem cells in theory can treat around 70 blood related disorders and genetic disorders including thalas- semia, sickle cell anaemia, leukaemia, and immune related disorders. x But given the present state of medicine, they are effective only for around a dozen of them. Are stem cells useful for family members? x Body’s immune system does not accept outside stem cells and other cells of the immune system. x Cord blood taken from a baby's umbilical cord is always a perfect match for the baby. x In addition, immediate family members are more likely to also be a match for the banked stem cells. x Hence, it may sometimes be possible to use the stem cells of the immediate family member to treat certain diseases. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 129 What does Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) say about cord blood banking? x Companies convince parents (emotional marketing) to bank the cells promising future therapeutic use. x However, the ICMR does not recommend commercial stem cell banking. x According to ICMR, there is no scientific basis for preservation of cord blood for future self use. x According to ICMR, cord blood banking is advisable when there is an elder child in the family with a condition treatable with stem cells and the mother is expecting the next baby. What do experts say? x Globally, cord blood banking is recommended as a source of hematopoietic stem cell (derived from bone marrow, umbilical cord) transplantation for haematological (diseases related to blood) cancers. x For all other conditions, the use of cord blood as a source of stem cells is not yet established. Digital India Project x PM announced 3 Digital India projects, National Digital Health Mission, a new Cyber Security Policy & promised optical fibre connectivity on Independence Day. Optical-Fibre Connectivity x BharatNet envisages laying of about 8 lakh kilometre of optical fibre cable (OFC) to all the 2,50,000-plus Gram Panchayats (GP) in the country at an estimated cost of Rs 42,068 crore ($6.2 billion). x It aims to provide speeds of upto 100 Mbps to all gram panchayats (GPs). x Initiated in October 2011, BharatNet was originally named National Optical Fibre Network or NOFN. x It’s being financed by the Universal Service Obligation Fund of the Department of Telecommunications, through a 5 per cent levy on the revenues of private telecom service providers. x The project’s primary objective is to extend fibre connectivity to every panchayat, thereby providing access to broadband internet services to 69 per cent of India’s rural population. x Phase I of BharatNet, which commenced in June 2014, was completed in December 2017. x In the Phase II, the remaining 1,29,827-gram panchayats are to be covered. x This phase incorporates a mix of both underground & aerial fibre as well as radio & satellite connectivity to reach more inaccessible locations such as Jammu & Kashmir, Northeast, Himachal Pradesh & Uttarakhand. x In the third phase from 2019 to 2023, state-of-the-art, future-proof network, including fiber between dis- tricts & blocks, with ring topology to provide redundancy would be created. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 130 x The project is a Centre-State collaborative project, with the States contributing free Rights of Way for estab- lishing the Optical Fibre Network National Digital Health Mission x The genesis of the new digital health infrastructure in India came about in the 2017 National Health Policy, which proposed a new National Digital Health Authority. x In August 2020, National Digital Health Mission (NDHM) released its latest strategic document, outlining the envisioned digital registries of doctors, hospitals, insurance companies, digital personal health records, etc. x The NDHM is a complete digital health ecosystem. x It will also include e-pharmacy & telemedicine services, regulatory guidelines for which are being framed. x The digital platform will be launched with four key features — health ID, personal health records, Digi Doctor & health facility registry. x Patients can create a Health ID, allowing them to share their data between hospitals & doctors digitally. x If individuals are looking to benefit from government schemes, then they will be required to connect their ID to their Aadhaar. x One copy of a patient’s records is stored in their doctor’s files & one is stored in their own individual locker (which can be owned by a company or by the government). x Other than the registry of doctors, professionals, & institutions, this allows for decentralised storing. x The NDHM is implemented by the National Health Authority (NHA) under the Health Ministry. x The platform will be available in the form of an app & website. x The vision is often compared to the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), a government-owned highway that private players can hook into to provide their applications to consumers. x NDHM is overseen by a Mission Steering Group with Ministers from IT, AYUSH, Women’s & Child Devel- opment, as well as Niti Aayog Member, NHA CEO, & others. National Health Policy 2017 x It envisages providing larger package of assured comprehensive primary health care through the ‘Health & Wellness Centres’. x It aims to allocate major proportion of resources to primary care & intends to ensure availability of two beds per 1,000 population distributed in a manner to enable access within golden hour. x Golden hour-the first hour after traumatic injury, when the victim is most likely to benefit from emergency treatment. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 131 x In addition, the policy proposes free drugs, free diagnostics & free emergency & essential health care ser- vices in all public hospitals in a bid to provide access & financial protection. x The policy proposes raising public health expenditure to 2.5 per cent of the GDP in a time-bound man- ner, the 2.5 per cent of GDP spend target for this sector would be met by 2025. x Among key targets, the policy intends to increase life expectancy at birth from 67.5 to 70 by 2025 & reduce infant mortality rate to 28 by 2019. x It also aims to reduce under five mortality to 23 by the year 2025. x Besides, it intends to achieve the global 2020 HIV target. Cybersecurity Policy 2020 x The new cybersecurity policy to be rolled in 2020 would replace the present one. x The existing policy, India’s first, was released in 2013. x Cyber intrusions & attacks have increased in scope & sophistication targeting sensitive personal & business data, & critical information infrastructure, with impact on national economy & security. x The present cyber threat landscape poses significant challenges due to rapid technological developments such as Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence, lnternet of Things (IoT), 5G, etc. x New challenges include data protection/privacy, law enforcement in evolving cyberspace, access to data stored overseas, misuse of social media, cooperation on cybercrime & cyber terrorism, & so on. x Threats from organised cybercriminal groups, technological cold wars, & increasing state sponsored cyber- attacks have also emerged. x Thus, a need exists for the formulation of a National Cyber Security Strategy 2020. National Cyber Security Strategy 2020 (NCSS 2020) x GOI under the aegis of National Security Council Secretariat is in the process of formulating the National Cyber Security Strategy 2020 to cater for a time horizon of five years (2020-25). x Proposed vision is to ensure a safe, secure, resilient & vibrant cyber space for our Nation’s prosperity. Pillars of Strategy x Examining various facets of cyber security under the following pillars: - a) Secure (The National Cyberspace) b) Strengthen (Structures, People, Processes, Capabilities) c) Synergise (Resources including Cooperation & Collaboration) PMF IAS – Learn Smart 132 Objectives of National Cyber Security Policy 1. To create a secure cyber ecosystem in the country. 2. To generate adequate trust & confidence in IT systems & transactions in cyberspace. 3. To create an assurance framework for design of security policies. 4. To strengthen the Regulatory framework for ensuring a Secure Cyberspace ecosystem. 5. To enhance the protection & resilience of Nation’s critical information infrastructure by operating a 24x7 National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC). 6. To develop suitable indigenous security technologies. 7. To improve visibility of the integrity of ICT products & services. 8. To create a workforce of 500,000 professionals skilled in cyber security in the next 5 years through capacity building, skill development & training. 9. To provide fiscal benefits to businesses for adoption of standard security practices & processes. 10. To enable protection of information while in process, handling, storage & transit so as to safeguard privacy of citizen's data & for reducing economic losses due to cyber-crime or data theft. 11. To enable effective prevention, investigation & prosecution of cyber-crime & enhancement of law. 12. To develop effective public private partnerships & collaborative engagements through technical & oper- ational cooperation & contribution for enhancing the security of cyberspace. 13. To enhance global cooperation by promoting shared understanding & leveraging relationships for fur- thering the cause of security of cyberspace. Diseases and Related Topics that are Frequently in News Antimicrobial resistance (AR) x The WHO defines antimicrobial resistance (antibiotic, antiviral or anti-malarial resistance) as a microorgan- ism's resistance to an antimicrobial drug that was once able to treat an infection by that microorganism. x E.g. In Multi Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB – resistant to multiple antimicrobials), the TB bacteria are resistant to two of the most important TB drugs, isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin (RMP). x Micro-organisms can develop resistance mainly in two ways: intrinsic resistance and acquired resistance. x Intrinsic resistance refers to the innate ability of an organism to resist a class of antimicrobial agents. x Acquired resistance refers to micro-organisms acquiring the gene coding (genetic mutation) for resistance. x Acquired resistance is more common than intrinsic resistance. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 133 Issues x Treating resistant microbes require alternative or higher doses of medication (expensive + toxic). x In 2016, upto 4,90,000 people developed multi-drug-resistant TB globally. x Drug resistance is starting to complicate the fight against HIV and malaria as well. x Organ transplantation, chemotherapy and surgeries would be compromised without effective antimicrobials. Causative measures x Overuse, misuse and improper use (e.g. taking antibiotics to treat viral diseases!) of antimicrobials. x Greater access to over the counter antibiotic drugs in developing countries. x Using broad-spectrum antibiotics over narrow-spectrum antibiotics (targeting specific microbes only). x Dumping of inadequately treated effluents from the pharmaceutical industry. x Antibiotic use in livestock feed at low doses for growth promotion is industrialized countries. x Poor sanitation and hygiene that forces the extended use of antimicrobials. Measures required x Global collective action through international treaties on antimicrobial resistance. x Preventing over the counter sale of antibiotics. x Swatch Baharat, awareness, etc. 2019-05: World’s rivers loaded with antibiotics waste x The concentrations of major antibiotics like Ciprofloxacin (treatment for intestinal and urinary tract infec- tions) and metronidazole in water bodies were several times above the limit in many parts of the world. x Discovered in the 1920s, antibiotics are used to treat pneumonia, tuberculosis, meningitis and a host of deadly bacteria. x Overuse and misuse of the drugs are thought to be the main causes of antimicrobial resistance. 2019-07: Colistin banned in animal food industry x The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has prohibited the manufacture, sale and distribution of colistin and its formulations for food-producing animals, poultry, aqua farming and animal feed supplements. x The move is a “massive victory” for the movement against anti-microbial resistance. x Colistin is a valuable, last-resort antibiotic that saves lives in critical care units. x In recent years, may patients have exhibited resistance to the drug. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 134 x Therefore, preventing arbitrary use of colistin in the food industry, particularly as growth supplements (growth factor) used in animals, poultry would likely reduce the antimicrobial resistance within the country. Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) x Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) in its current form has been introduced in India in 1985. x Ministry of Health provides several vaccines to infants, children and pregnant women through UIP. Immunization x Immunization is the process through which a person is made immune to an infectious disease. x Immunization typically involves administration of a vaccine. x Vaccines stimulate the body’s own immune system to protect against subsequent infection or disease. Vaccines provided under UIP x OPV is given orally in the form of two drops. x Rotavirus vaccine is given orally in the form of 5 drops. x Rest of the vaccines under UIP are administered through injections. Bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccine (BCG) x It is given to infants to protect them from tubercular meningitis and disseminated TB. x BCG vaccine is given at birth or as early as possible before one year. Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) x OPV stands for Oral Polio Vaccine. x It protects children from poliomyelitis. x OPV is given at birth called zero dose and three doses are given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. x A booster dose is given at 16-24 months of age. Hepatitis B vaccine x Hepatitis B vaccine protects from Hepatitis B virus infection. x Hepatitis B vaccine is given at birth or as early as possible within 24 hours. x Subsequently 3 doses are given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks in combination with DPT and Hib in the form of pentavalent vaccine. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 135 Pentavalent Vaccine x Pentavalent vaccine is a combined vaccine to protect children from five diseases Diphtheria, Tetanus, Per- tussis, Haemophilic influenza type b infection and Hepatitis B. x Three doses are given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of age (can be given till one year of age). Rotavirus Vaccine (RV) x It gives protection to infants and children against rotavirus diarrhoea. x It is given in select states. x Three doses of vaccine are given at 6, 10, 14 weeks of age. Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV) x PCV stands for. x It protects infants and young children against disease caused by the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae. x It is given in select states. x The vaccine is given as two primary doses at 6 & 14 weeks followed by a booster dose at 9 months. Fractional Inactivated Poliomyelitis Vaccine (fIPV) x It is used to boost the protection against poliomyelitis (polio). x Two fractional doses of IVP are given intradermally at 6 and 14 weeks of age. Measles, Rubella (MR) vaccine x In few states, a combined vaccine is given to protect from Measles and Rubella infection. x First dose is given at 9 completed months and second dose is given at 16-24 months. Japanese encephalitis vaccine (JE) x It gives protection against Japanese Encephalitis. x JE vaccine is given in select districts endemic for JE. x First dose is given at 9 completed months and second dose at 16-24 months of age. DPT booster x DPT is a combined vaccine; it protects children from Diphtheria, Tetanus and Pertussis. x DPT first booster is given at 16-24 months of age and DPT 2nd booster is given at 5-6 years of age. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 136 Tetanus toxoid vaccine (TT) x TT is used to provide protection against tetanus. x Tetanus toxoid vaccine is given at 10 years and 15 years of age. x Pregnant women-TT-1 is given early in pregnancy; and TT-2 is given 4 weeks after TT-1. Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES) x Bihar loses hundreds of children aged between 2 to 10 years to AES every year. x AES is a collective term used for referring to neurological manifestations which include mental confusion, disorientation, convulsion (sudden movement caused by involuntary contraction of muscles), coma, etc. x Meningitis caused by virus or bacteria, encephalitis (mostly Japanese encephalitis) caused by virus, encepha- lopathy, cerebral malaria, etc. are collectively called acute encephalitis syndrome. x While microbes cause encephalitis, encephalopathy is biochemical in origin. x Encephalitis: An inflammation of brain cells due to a viral or bacterial infection. x Encephalopathy: brain damage caused due to an environmental toxin. x There are different types of encephalopathy. In the present case, it is associated with hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar level) and hence called hypoglycaemic encephalopathy. x Unlike hypoglycaemic encephalopathy, encephalitis does not cause low blood sugar level. The link between hypoglycaemic encephalopathy (HE) and litchi x The spike in AES cases is a result of malnourished children suffering brain damage after eating litchis. x Litchis contain a chemical called methylene cyclopropyl glycine (MCPG). x These are naturally occurring toxins that cause hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar level) in children. x In malnourished children, when the reserves of glucose from the digestive tract and the liver are exhausted, fatty acids are oxidized to supply blood sugar to the brain. MCPG toxin thwarts this mechanism. x This can send the brain into hypoglycaemic shock triggering convulsions and, if unaddressed, even death. Treatment x Complete recovery can be achieved if affected children are infused with 10% dextrose within four hours after the onset of symptoms. x Infusing 10% dextrose restores blood sugar to a safe level and also stops the production of amino acid that is toxic to brain cells by shutting down the body’s attempt to convert fatty acid into glucose. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 137 Measures to be taken to prevent similar health crisis in future x Overhauling the healthcare apparatus to deal with a crisis of this magnitude. x Local public healthcare centres must stock up anti-convulsion drugs as well as dextrose. x The state must effectively implement schemes that provide nutritious food to children. x The public must be sensitised about the causes of AES and the necessary preventive measures to be taken. Diabetes x Diabetes is a chronic disease that occurs either when 9 the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or 9 when the body cannot effectively use the insulin it produces. x Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood sugar. x Hyperglycaemia, or raised blood sugar, is a common effect of uncontrolled diabetes and over time leads to serious damage to many of the body's systems, especially the nerves and blood vessels. Type 1 diabetes x Type 1 diabetes is characterized by deficient insulin production and requires daily administration of insulin. x Neither the cause of Type 1 diabetes nor the means to prevent it are known. Type 2 diabetes x Type 2 diabetes results from the body’s ineffective use of insulin. x The majority of people with diabetes have type 2 diabetes. x This type of diabetes is largely the result of excess body weight and physical inactivity. x Until recently, this type of diabetes was seen only in adults, but it is now increasingly occurring in children. Gestational diabetes x Gestational diabetes is hyperglycaemia where blood sugar levels are below those diagnosed of diabetes. x Gestational diabetes occurs during pregnancy. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 138 Source and Credits Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) x Ebola virus was first discovered in 1970s near the Ebola River in the Democratic Republic of Congo. x Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) is a disease in people and nonhuman primates (monkeys, gorillas, chimpanzees). x The viruses that cause EVD are located mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 139 x Ebola virus spreads through direct contact with an infected person or through direct contact with an infected animal (bat or nonhuman primate). x There is no approved vaccine or treatment for EVD. x A vaccine was found to be effective (97.5% efficacy) in a trials conducted by WHO. But it is not yet approved. x Symptoms of EVD include fever, headache, muscle pain, weakness, fatigue, diarrhoea, etc. x Diagnosing can be difficult as early symptoms are not specific to Ebola virus infection. x Recovery from EVD depends on good supportive care and the patient’s immune response. x Ebola survivors may experience difficult side effects after their recovery, such as tiredness, muscle aches, etc. Hepatitis x Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver. x It is caused by Virus. x Hepatitis viruses are the most common cause of hepatitis in the world but other infections, toxic substances (e.g., alcohol, certain drugs), and autoimmune diseases can also cause hepatitis. x There are 5 main hepatitis viruses, referred to as types A, B, C, D and E. x In particular, types B and C lead to chronic disease in hundreds of millions of people and, together, are the most common cause of liver cirrhosis and cancer. x Hepatitis A and E are typically caused by ingestion of contaminated food or water. x Hepatitis B, C and D usually occur as a result of parenteral contact with infected body fluids. x Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is mostly transmitted through exposure to infective blood. x This may happen through transfusions of HCV-contaminated blood and blood products, contaminated in- jections during medical procedures, and through injection drug use. x Sexual transmission is also possible, but is much less common. x There is no vaccine for HCV. Answer: b) Influenza (Flu) x Flu is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses that infect the nose, throat, and some- times the lungs. x It can cause mild to severe illness, and at times can lead to death. x There are four types of influenza viruses namely A, B, C and D. 1. Influenza A viruses: These are the only influenza viruses that cause flu pandemics that is global epi- demics of flu disease. 2. Influenza B viruses: They are not classified into subtypes and can be broken down into lineages. 3. Influenza C viruses: This type of virus is detected less frequently and usually causes mild infections and does not present public health risk. Or we can say that they do not cause human flu epidemic. 4. Influenza D viruses: They primarily affect cattle and does not infect or cause illness in people. x Influenza A and B viruses causes acute respiratory infection and the seasonal epidemic of disease. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 141 Source and Credits Nipah virus x The Nipah virus was first recognised in 1999 during an outbreak among pig farmers in Malaysia. x The disease has also been identified periodically in Kerala. Nipah virus infection x The virus belongs to a new genus termed Henipavirus. x Nipah is an RNA or Ribonucleic Acid virus. x RNA viruses (most common cause diseases in humans) have high mutation rate compared to DNA viruses. Transmission x Nipah virus infection is a zoonosis (disease transmitted from animals to humans). x A zoonosis could be caused by a virus, bacteria, fungi or parasite; some examples include anthrax, bird flu, ebola, dengue, rabies, malaria, swine flu, etc. x Fruit bats (flying fox) (eat fruits and live in trees) are the natural hosts for Nipah virus. x Nipah transmission takes place when one consumes infected fruits and fresh date palm. x Loss of the natural habitat of the bats is exacerbating the rate of bat-to-human transmission. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 142 x As the flying fox habitat is destroyed, their immune system gets weaker, their virus load goes up. x Human-to-human transmission occurs due to direct contact. Symptoms x The incubation period (interval from infection to the onset of symptoms) ranges from four to 14 days. x Symptoms are similar to that of influenza: fever, muscle pain, and respiratory problems. x Headaches, dizziness, encephalitis (brain inflammation), etc. x Sometimes a person can have an asymptomatic infection (acts as a carrier without showing any symptoms). Treatment x There are currently no drugs or vaccines specific for the infection. Plasmodium Vivax Malaria TH | GS3 > Health x Context: Recently, an international team has developed a system to breed the parasite Plasmodium vivax in the lab & then infect cultured human liver cells with it. x Plasmodium vivax is a protozoal, parasite & a human pathogen. x This parasite is the most frequent & widely distributed cause of recurring malaria. x P. vivax is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito; the males do not bite. x Mosquitoes inject the sporozoite of the parasite into the skin & the sporozoites travel to the liver. x The parasite can remain in the liver in a dormant stage & relapse later. x Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, & Pakistan account for more than 80% of estimated cases of P. vivax. x Although it is less virulent than Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest of the five human malaria parasites, P. vivax malaria infections can lead to severe disease & death. x Certain malaria-endemic countries have even abandoned chloroquine for P. vivax treatment but fortunately chloroquine is still effective in India. Mosquito-Borne Diseases x Mosquito-borne diseases are those spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. x Diseases that are spread to people by mosquitoes include Zika virus, West Nile virus, Chikungunya virus, dengue, & malaria. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 143 Link: Source & Credits Pneumonia x Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that affects the lungs x It is most commonly caused by viruses, bacteria and fungi. x The lungs are made up of small sacs called alveoli, which fill with air when a healthy person breathes. x When an individual has pneumonia, the alveoli are filled with pus and fluid, which makes breathing painful and limits oxygen intake. x These infections are generally spread by direct contact with infected people. Rotavirus x Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea and death among children under the age of five. x Rotavirus is a highly contagious virus. x Rotavirus transmission occurs primarily by the faecal-oral route, or indirectly via contaminated fomites. x In India, around 78,000 children die from Rotavirus diarrhoea annually. x It is estimated that Rotavirus accounts for 40% of the hospitalisation among children in India. x Diarrhoea causes 9.2% of the total deaths among children under five years. x If not treated adequately, it may result in dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, shock and death. Sickle Cell Anemia What is Thalassemia? PMF IAS – Learn Smart 144 x Thalassemia is an inherited (i.e., passed from parents to children through genes) blood disorder caused when the body doesn’t make enough of a protein called hemoglobin, an important part of red blood cells. x When there isn’t enough hemoglobin, the body’s red blood cells don’t function properly & they last shorter periods of time, so there are fewer healthy red blood cells traveling in the bloodstream. x Red blood cells carry oxygen to all the cells of the body. x Oxygen is a sort of food that cells use to function. x When there are not enough healthy red blood cells, there is also not enough oxygen delivered to all the other cells of the body, which may cause a person to feel tired, weak or short of breath. This is a condition called anemia. x People with thalassemia may have mild or severe anemia. x Severe anemia can damage organs & lead to death.
